draft: The text calls for a repeated festival. That alone does not show when each part began or how widely people followed it. It also does not prove that the departure happened.
meaningCheck: Keeps separate limits on the festival’s origins, its practice, and the historical departure.

draft: Finds from ancient sites and ancestry changes shown by DNA raise a question about the Philistines named in Genesis. Were they the same people known from later history, placed in an earlier setting? Ashkelon is not Gerar. A DNA sample does not define everyone who bore a name. The story may also use later terms for places.
meaningCheck: Preserves the proposed identification as a question, site difference, sample limit, and possible later geographical wording.

draft: The old Greek translation differs from the KJV of Nehemiah 7 in five entries. It gives Pahathmoab 2,618 people, where the KJV gives 2,818. After Hariph, it adds “the children of Asen, 223”. It lists Bethlehem with 123 and Netophah with 56; the KJV gives one total of 188. For “the other Nebo”, it gives 152 rather than 52. For “the other Elam”, it gives 1,252 rather than 1,254.
meaningCheck: Check all five contrasts and each number; the old Greek translation means the cited Brenton edition only.

draft: The text alone cannot prove that the ceremony happened at a known date. It cannot show every ritual detail or establish who wrote the final work and how it was passed down.
meaningCheck: Keeps the event-date, ritual-detail, authorship, and transmission limits.

draft: The shared wording shows that the later text reuses Scripture. Its conclusion about belief argues for an interpretation. It does not give a second account of the original ceremony.
meaningCheck: Keeps direct reuse distinct from the later theological argument and from a second ceremony account.

draft: Named officials and a date within a king’s reign set the scene. The message explains the weather as God’s work. It does not provide an independent study of the weather.
meaningCheck: Retains narrative dating and divine causation as the message’s explanation, not demonstrated weather science.

draft: This comparison identifies the wording and a reading based on its context. It does not show that all ancient readers made this distinction. It does not settle whether religious images are right or wrong.
meaningCheck: Preserves the contextual interpretation, reader-diversity limit, and unresolved ethics.

draft: The story does not independently show the troop numbers or battle date. Its religious explanation of victory is not a tested account of how the army won. It does not settle whether endless hostility is right or wrong.
meaningCheck: Retains number/date limits, lack of an experimental military explanation, and the ethical limit on perpetual hostility.

draft: The anger may concern Balaam’s motive or the way he acts. The story does not clearly give one full reason why anger follows permission.
meaningCheck: Keeps motive and manner as possible readings, not an established explanation.

draft: The texts conflict if Ecclesiastes denies all future life. Yet Ecclesiastes repeatedly focuses on life on earth. This allows a distinction between being inactive now and waking in the future.
meaningCheck: Keeps the conflict conditional and the earthly-perspective reading possible.

draft: The account says the act was not commanded. It does not fully state which rule was broken. It does not independently confirm the deaths or show how a natural process caused them.
meaningCheck: Retains the uncommanded act and separate procedural, historical, and natural-mechanism limits.

draft: This comparison tests a recent reading in which all people descend only from this family, through normal inheritance. DNA evidence supports a much older history with groups of ancestors. Other cited studies test how a sharp population fall would reduce differences across several kinds of DNA. The paper does not directly model an eight-person flood population. This comparison uses both its account of past populations and the separate study of a sharp population fall. The Adam-and-Eve sources give context for a recent reading in which all people descend only from one couple.
meaningCheck: Keeps the exclusive recent-family assumption, ordinary inheritance, multiple genetic systems, and absence of a direct eight-person simulation.

draft: The editions name different places left behind: πόλεως, city, and πύλης, gate. They also differ over who supposed something. One has ἐνομίζετο, it was supposed. The other has ἐνομίζομεν, we supposed.
meaningCheck: Preserves both place words, both verb forms, and the change in grammatical subject.

draft: The story gives an order of events and a religious explanation. It does not name the wood, water chemistry, or dose. It does not give a treatment that others can repeat.
meaningCheck: Retains sequence and theological explanation, plus each missing treatment detail.

draft: This describes how the law presents guilt. It does not judge blame by modern standards or show that the law was enforced the same way everywhere. It is not a full account of forgiveness.
meaningCheck: Retains the legal framing and separate limits on modern culpability, enforcement, and forgiveness.

draft: Both passages are in one letter. In 11:5, a rule for a woman who prays or prophesies assumes that she does so. In 14:34, women must keep silent and may not speak in the churches. Both can stand if 11:5 concerns prayer and prophecy outside the gathering. Another reading limits 14:34 to weighing prophecies (14:29–33) or asking questions in the gathering (14:35). Neither verse states these limits directly.
meaningCheck: Keeps all three possible reconciliations and the explicit limit that neither verse states them.

draft: At 15:9, Hebrew has נוֹסָפוֹת (“more”) and אַרְיֵה, a lion. The KJV gives “more” and “lions”. Greek gives “Arabians” in the first place and “Ariel” in the second. Greek ends with the place name Adama. The KJV has “the land” (אֲדָמָה).
meaningCheck: Preserves the quoted Hebrew exactly, both Greek contrasts, and Adama as the Greek place name.

draft: The figure is first called “a man”. He then gives a title found in the KJV only in these two verses. Joshua falls on his face and calls him “my Lord”. Is the figure a human officer, an angel, or God? This affects how we read Joshua’s act and who speaks next. The three verses give no message from the captain beyond the command about the shoe. A verse about Jericho being shut up follows. The next instructions begin with “And the Lord said unto Joshua”.
meaningCheck: Retains all three identity options, the limited captain speech, and the stated sequence before the next speaker.

draft: The story credits Moses with writing. This shows the book’s own claim, rather than outside proof that he wrote the whole surviving book. The closing narrator’s viewpoint differs from the earlier claim about Moses writing the law. This distinction alone does not identify an author, editor, or date.
meaningCheck: Keeps internal authorship attribution separate from external proof; does not infer an author, editor, or date.

draft: These choices apply to the cases discussed here. They do not prove that all required sacrifices allowed the same substitutes. They do not show how much wealth ancient households had.
meaningCheck: Retains the case limit, non-universal substitutes, and household-wealth limit.

draft: A known modern illness makes a natural explanation possible. Yet eating similar food does not prove that the story describes the same disease.
meaningCheck: Keeps a natural explanation possible and resemblance insufficient for diagnosis.

draft: The editions differ over who will know whose affairs. In one, the verb means he may know, and the pronoun is “you”. In the other, the verb means you may know, addressing several people, and the pronoun is “us”.
meaningCheck: Preserves singular he versus plural you and the you/us change without dropping the grammatical distinction.

draft: The editions begin the verse with different words. One has δή … οὐ συμφέρει μοι, meaning indeed it is not expedient for me. The other has δεῖ, meaning it is necessary, with οὐ συμφέρον μέν, meaning not profitable, indeed.
meaningCheck: Preserves both exact Greek sequences and all supplied English meanings.

draft: The permissions differ if read as one unchanged rule for the same circumstances. Deuteronomy frames its rules around settled life, larger territory, and distance. The move from wilderness to settled life may explain the change.
meaningCheck: Keeps the conflict conditional and the contextual explanation possible.

draft: Two accounts of one escape name different groups seeking Paul. One names Jews who planned to kill him. The other names King Aretas’s governor, who guarded the city to seize him. Both can stand if the Jews acted through the governor or asked him to set the guard. They can also stand if both groups sought Paul. Neither passage says this. Acts names neither Aretas nor a military guard. Second Corinthians does not mention the Jews.
meaningCheck: Retains the two stated parties, all three possible reconciliations, and both passages’ omissions.

draft: The story states this condition and reports that it was met at the crossing. This does not independently confirm the force’s size, the dates, or how much land was settled.
meaningCheck: Keeps narrative fulfillment distinct from independent support for numbers, chronology, and settlement extent.

draft: The passage shows the system described in the text. It does not independently prove that a known population used this system at a known date. It does not show that its numbered ranks were used the same way everywhere.
meaningCheck: Retains the textual evidence, historical verification limit, and limit on uniform use of numerical tiers.

draft: The shared names support comparing the groups and ties shown in these writings. The texts alone cannot establish every life story or settle who wrote them.
meaningCheck: Keeps the social-network comparison and limits on biographies and authorship.

draft: These clues support reading the selected phrases as images. They need not claim that words are liquid, God is a mineral, or arrows process alcohol like living things.
meaningCheck: Retains the figurative reading and all three literal claims it avoids.

draft: The law gives a schedule and warns of danger. This does not independently show that people followed it or explain a bodily cause of death. It does not show every detail of later temple practice.
meaningCheck: Preserves the schedule/danger framing and limits on observance, biological causation, and later practice.

draft: The text gives the rule within the story. Whether people enforced it, and whether it was right, need separate study. The scene does not clearly state the man’s inner motive. The earlier category of defiance does not, by itself, give a full account of that motive.
meaningCheck: Keeps historical enforcement and ethics separate and avoids assigning a motive from the preceding category.

draft: Greek edition 2 has a clause about someone who does not regard the day. It comes between the clauses about someone who regards it and someone who eats. Greek edition 1 moves straight from one to the other.
meaningCheck: Source aliases retain Textus Receptus as edition 2 and Tischendorf as edition 1; clause position and omission stay unchanged.

draft: This compares parts of the story. It does not independently confirm an Egyptian order, identify a pharaoh, or prove that the rescue happened. The midwives’ explanation in 1:19 states what characters say. It is not medical evidence about childbirth.
meaningCheck: Preserves internal comparison, all three historical limits, and the status of the midwives’ statement.

draft: Calling something evidence in law does not make it scientific proof of sexual history. Modern medical findings challenge using bodily signs to prove virginity. They do not decide whether a specific ancient accusation was true.
meaningCheck: Retains the legal/scientific distinction and avoids deciding a particular ancient case.

draft: The shared words directly show a link between the texts. They alone do not show who borrowed from whom or rule out a shared tradition.
meaningCheck: Preserves direct evidence of textual relationship while retaining borrowing-direction and common-tradition limits.

draft: Two changed word endings change what the verse compares. In one edition, the Father is greater than all. In the other, what the Father has given is greater than all.
meaningCheck: Retains the two endings and precisely identifies each grammatical subject.

draft: The story’s actions are in tension with its stated policy. This does not prove that the laws contradict themselves. Deception and the oath explain the story’s decision. They do not independently prove its legal force, show it happened, or settle whether forced service was just.
meaningCheck: Keeps policy/conduct tension separate from contradictory laws and preserves legal, historical, and ethical limits.

draft: This does not infer a minimum headcount, an exact date for a sharp population fall, or exclude every ancestral couple. A genetic estimate of population size is not a literal headcount. A couple or family could be ancestors through family lines within a larger population; that is a different claim. Survival in one region, literary readings, and religious readings also make different claims. The cited study does not test miraculous creation or the miraculous return of genetic variety.
meaningCheck: Preserves the census/effective-size distinction, genealogical ancestry alternative, regional/literary/theological alternatives, and miracle limit.

draft: This identifies unequal ritual rules. It does not show that the body takes twice as long to recover after a daughter. It cannot explain the rules’ historical reason or settle whether they were right.
meaningCheck: Keeps the unequal prescription, no doubled biological recovery claim, and historical/ethical limits.

draft: Genesis 18:11 may refer to the end of Sarah’s periods. If so, aging helps explain why the story presents the promised birth as unusual. Modern facts about menopause cannot, by themselves, diagnose Sarah. They do not show how natural conception occurred in this account or test the divine action it describes. The context keeps that distinction. It does not treat an unspecified miracle as an event disproved by science.
meaningCheck: Keeps the initial conditional reading and all three limits on medical comparison and divine action.

draft: Joshua itself gives Jerusalem as an exception. Judges lists more places that were not conquered. Language about total victory need not mean that every settlement was occupied or every person killed. The stated exception limits a reading that allows no exceptions to the destruction. It does not show the full historical extent of conquest or settle whether the killings were right.
meaningCheck: Retains Jerusalem, the additional places, non-universal military language, and historical/ethical limits.

draft: After “conscience”, one edition adds τοῦ γὰρ κυρίου ἡ γῆ καὶ τὸ πλήρωμα αὐτῆς. This means for the earth is the Lord’s and its fulness. These are words from Psalm 24:1, already given in 10:26. The other edition ends the verse at “conscience”.
meaningCheck: Preserves the exact Greek sequence, supplied meaning, both source references, and different verse endings.

draft: This gives a religious reading of a promise about descendants. The chapter itself applies the promise both to one person and to a group.
meaningCheck: Retains theological rereading and both individual and collective applications.

draft: This conclusion applies to this vision. It does not judge every other image in Revelation as a claim about science or history.
meaningCheck: Keeps the conclusion limited to this vision without a blanket verdict elsewhere.

draft: The ingredients show what this passage calls a meat offering. Reading that name as always meaning animal flesh would misread the recipe.
meaningCheck: Keeps the recipe-based meaning and rejects only the necessarily-animal-flesh reading.

draft: Both verses use the Greek verb for “be justified”, together with the law and doing. One says people who do the law will be justified. The other says no flesh will be justified by works of the law. They can stand together if 2:13 describes what the law’s own standard requires. Romans 3:9–20 then says all are under sin. Another reading takes 2:13 to mean a different kind of doer. Neither verse states these explanations in its own words.
meaningCheck: Retains shared Greek wording, both contrasting claims, both possible reconciliations, and the limit on what the verses state.

draft: Verses 15:7–8 name the region up to Shur and say all the people were destroyed. In 27:8, Amalekites live in the region toward Shur. In 30:1, an Amalekite force can sack a town.
meaningCheck: Preserves the three references, location, totalizing destruction wording, and later raiding capacity.

draft: This compares rules in the texts. It does not advise anyone to stay in an unsafe relationship or decide modern legal rights.
meaningCheck: Keeps both the safety and modern-law limits without adding guidance.

draft: The restriction on release gives a real protection in the text. It does not show equal power to negotiate or clear consent during wartime captivity.
meaningCheck: Retains the textual protection without treating it as equal bargaining power or explicit consent.
